question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A poll taken of voters leaving the voting place that is usually used for predicting the winners.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Exit poll.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Exit poll" means a poll taken of voters immediately after they have left the polling booth, used to predict the likely result of an election before the official count. (मतदान के तुरंत बाद लिया गया सर्वेक्षण जो चुनाव परिणाम का अनुमान लगाने हेतु किया जाता है)
◦ Example: According to the exit poll, the ruling party is expected to win a comfortable majority.

• The word is formed from "exit" (leaving) + "poll" (a survey of opinion), literally a survey conducted as voters exit the polling station.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Consensus (सर्वसम्मति): General agreement among a group of people; it has nothing to do with predicting election results.

• Option 2: Results: The final, official outcome of an election announced after counting of votes — not a prediction made beforehand.

• Option 3: Census (जनगणना): An official count or survey of a population, usually to record demographic data; unrelated to voting predictions.

NOTE

• Related election vocabulary often tested by SSC: "Opinion poll" (a survey of public opinion taken before an election), "Bogus voting" (illegal impersonation while voting), "Franchise" (the right to vote), and "Suffrage" (the right to vote in political elections).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Intense
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Moderate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Intense" means existing in an extreme degree; very strong, forceful or concentrated. (अत्यधिक तीव्र)
◦ Example: The intense heat of the desert made travelling difficult.

• Its antonym "Moderate" means average in amount, intensity or degree; not extreme. (मध्यम, संयत)
◦ Example: He prefers moderate exercise rather than intense workouts.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Thrifty (मितव्ययी): Careful with money; economical. This describes a spending habit, not degree/intensity, so it is not an antonym of "intense".

• Option 3: Stately (भव्य, गरिमापूर्ण): Dignified and impressive in appearance; unrelated to intensity.

• Option 4: Lavish (उदार, अत्यधिक खर्चीला): Given or spent in great amounts; this is actually closer in spirit to "intense" (excessive) rather than its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "intense": acute, fierce, extreme, severe, vehement.

• Other antonyms of "intense": mild, gentle, calm, slight.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Usually, Ratheesh hasn’t / take part in these types / of events because of / his hectic schedule.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Usually, Ratheesh hasn’t.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The adverb "Usually" indicates a habitual or routine action and must be used with the Simple Present Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule: Adverbs of habitual frequency such as "usually", "generally", "normally", "often" are followed by a verb in the Simple Present (Subject + do/does + not + V1), not by "has/have + not + V3" (Present Perfect).

• Since the sentence describes Ratheesh’s habitual behaviour ("usually...because of his hectic schedule"), the auxiliary should be "doesn’t", not "hasn’t". Hence the segment "Usually, Ratheesh hasn’t" is grammatically inconsistent with the rest of the sentence.

• Corrected sentence: "Usually, Ratheesh doesn’t take part in these types of events because of his hectic schedule."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "take part in these types" is grammatically fine as a base-form verb phrase once the auxiliary is corrected to "doesn’t".

• Option 2: "of events because of" is a correct prepositional phrase and contains no error.

• Option 3: "his hectic schedule" is a correct noun phrase and contains no error.

NOTE

• Other habitual-frequency adverbs that require Simple Present: always, sometimes, seldom, rarely, every day/week/year.

• Do not confuse this with sentences using "never" with Present Perfect (e.g., "I have never seen such a mess"), which is a separate, valid construction expressing an experience up to now.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
There was a _____________accident last night and the inspector on deputy was unable to raise help when she called from the mountains.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. serious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Serious" means grave, significant or dangerous in nature, and is the standard collocation used with the word "accident" when describing an event severe enough to need emergency help.
◦ Example: There was a serious accident on the highway, and two ambulances were called.

• The context — "the inspector...was unable to raise help when she called from the mountains" — implies the accident was grave and urgent, which fits "serious accident" as a natural collocation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "goofy" means silly or foolish; it does not collocate with "accident" and makes no sense in this context.

• Option 2: "gloomy" means dark, dismal or depressing (usually describing mood or weather); it does not fit an "accident".

• Option 4: "harsh" means severe or rough (usually describing treatment, weather or criticism); "harsh accident" is not an idiomatic English collocation.

NOTE

• Common adjective-noun collocations tested by SSC: "serious illness/injury/accident", "severe weather/pain", "heavy rainfall/traffic", "grave danger/mistake".

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Distant
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Faraway.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Distant" means far away in space or time; not close. (दूर, दूरस्थ)
◦ Example: They could see the distant mountains from their window.

• "Faraway" carries the same meaning — located a long way off. (दूरस्थ, बहुत दूर)
◦ Example: She dreamt of travelling to faraway lands.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Farsighted (दूरदर्शी): Able to anticipate future needs/events wisely, or (medically) able to see distant objects clearly while near objects are blurred — describes vision/wisdom, not physical distance.

• Option 3: Futuristic (भविष्यवादी): Relating to the future or very modern in design; refers to time/style, not spatial distance.

• Option 4: Forward (आगे): Directed or moving ahead/onward; refers to direction, not remoteness.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "distant": remote, far-off, removed.

• Do not confuse "distant" (far away) with "distinct" (clearly different/separate) — a common SSC trap pair.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
They decided to have a meeting to discuss about the project.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. to discuss the project.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The verb "discuss" is a transitive verb and takes a direct object directly, without any preposition after it.

• Rule: Never use "about", "regarding" or "concerning" after "discuss" — say "discuss something", not "discuss about something".
◦ Example (correct): Let's discuss the matter tomorrow.
◦ Example (incorrect): Let's discuss about the matter tomorrow.

• Applying the rule, "to discuss about the project" must be corrected to "to discuss the project".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "to discuss through the project" wrongly inserts the preposition "through", which is not used with "discuss" and distorts the meaning.

• Option 3: "to discuss over the project" wrongly inserts "over"; "discuss" never takes a preposition before its object.

• Option 4: "to discuss beyond the project" wrongly inserts "beyond", which is meaningless in this context.

NOTE

• Other verbs commonly misused with an unnecessary preposition by SSC candidates: "emphasize" (not "emphasize on" — though "lay emphasis on" is correct), "request" (not "request for", though "make a request for" is fine), "reach" (not "reach to"), "marry" (not "marry with").

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A formal statement testifying to someone's character and qualifications
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Testimonial.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Testimonial" means a formal statement or certificate testifying to a person's character, conduct or qualifications. (चरित्र प्रमाण पत्र)
◦ Example: He submitted testimonials from his previous employers along with his job application.

• It is derived from "testify" — to give evidence or bear witness in favour of someone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Document (दस्तावेज़): Any official paper providing information or evidence; a very general term, not specifically about character/qualifications.

• Option 2: Affidavit (शपथ पत्र): A written statement confirmed by oath, used as evidence in court — not specifically about praising someone's character/qualifications.

• Option 4: Manuscript (हस्तलिपि): A handwritten or typed document, especially an author's original text before publication; unrelated to testifying character.

NOTE

• Other commonly tested one-word substitutes: "Curriculum Vitae/Resume" (a summary of one's qualifications and experience), "Reference" (a person who provides a testimonial), "Credentials" (qualifications/achievements that prove someone is entitled to trust).

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
The poor woman is in excruciating mental anguish, and her loved ones appear to have assisted in exarcerbating her traumatic experiences.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. exarcerbating.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "exacerbating" — from the verb "exacerbate", meaning to make a problem, situation or feeling worse.
◦ Example: Ignoring the wound only exacerbated the infection.

• Spelling key: EX + ACER + BATE. The given word wrongly inserts an extra "r" after "exa-", giving "exar-cerbating" instead of the correct "exa-cerbating".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "anguish" is spelt correctly — meaning severe mental or physical pain.

• Option 2: "excruciating" is spelt correctly — meaning intensely painful.

• Option 4: "traumatic" is spelt correctly — meaning deeply disturbing or distressing.

NOTE

• The word "exacerbate" is often confused with "exasperate" (to irritate or annoy greatly) — the two have different meanings though similar spellings.

• Other commonly misspelt words with silent/extra letters: accommodate, embarrass, occurrence, harass, questionnaire.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
As there were reports of manipulation of scores in the previous exams, the aspirants demanded a process to ensure________ assessment for selection.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. fair and square.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "fair and square" means honest, just and without cheating or trickery. (ईमानदारी और न्यायपूर्ण ढंग से)
◦ Example: He won the election fair and square, with no allegations of rigging.

• Since the aspirants were worried about "manipulation of scores", they would naturally demand an assessment process that is honest and free from unfair practices — i.e., conducted "fair and square".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "will o' the wisp" (मृगतृष्णा, भ्रामक वस्तु): Something illusory or deceptive that cannot be reached or achieved; refers to a delusive hope, not honesty in assessment.

• Option 2: "hole and corner" (गुप्त, छिपकर किया गया): Secretive or clandestine, done in an underhand manner — the opposite of the transparent assessment the aspirants wanted.

• Option 3: "well off" (संपन्न, धनी): In a good financial position; wealthy — unrelated to the fairness of an assessment process.

NOTE

• Other idioms of honesty/fairness often asked in SSC: "Above board" (open and legitimate), "On the level" (honest, truthful), "Play fair" (to act honestly and by the rules).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The party was a ________ hour for everyone, except Mukesh.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. happy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "happy hour" here is used to mean a joyful or pleasant period of time, and the sentence contrasts this happiness with Mukesh, who is implied to be the exception (not happy).
◦ Example: The reunion was a happy hour for the whole family, except for the one member who couldn't attend.

• The structure "a ___ hour for everyone, except X" requires a word describing an emotional state that can be true for most people but not for X — "happy" fits this logically and idiomatically.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "welcome" as an adjective means "gladly received", but "a welcome hour" is not a natural or idiomatic English expression in this context.

• Option 3: "dry" means without alcohol/moisture or (informally) dull; "a dry hour for everyone" does not fit the context of a party contrasted with one unhappy person.

• Option 4: "stable" means steady or unchanging; it does not describe an emotional experience of a party and does not fit the sentence.

NOTE

• Note the difference between "happy hour" as used here (a time of general enjoyment) and its common commercial sense (a period when discounted drinks are served at a bar) — SSC questions often test contextual, not literal/dictionary, meaning.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
Suman was taking a nap
option_1: A nap was being taken by Suman.
option_2: A nap has been taken by Suman.
option_3: A nap is being taken by Suman.
option_4: A nap was taken by Suman.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. A nap was being taken by Suman.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Suman was taking a nap" is in the Past Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + was/were + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "a nap" becomes the subject; since it is singular, the auxiliary is "was"; "being" is inserted; "taking" becomes the past participle "taken"; and "Suman" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: A nap was being taken by Suman.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has been taken" is the passive form of the Present Perfect Tense, not the Past Continuous.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is being taken" is the passive form of the Present Continuous Tense, not the Past Continuous.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "was taken" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense; it omits the continuous aspect ("being") required to show an action in progress.

NOTE

• A quick way to remember: Continuous tense passives always contain "being", and the "be" verb (was/were/is/am/are) must agree with the tense and number of the new subject.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Hold water
option_2: Appear to be of no value
option_4: Appear to be valid or reasonable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Appear to be valid or reasonable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "hold water" means (of a theory, argument or excuse) to appear to be true, valid or sound when examined; it is most often used in the negative — "doesn't hold water" — to say an argument is not convincing. (तर्कसंगत प्रतीत होना)
◦ Example: His explanation for being late simply doesn't hold water.

• The idiom derives from testing a container for leaks: if it can "hold water" without leaking, it is sound and reliable — just like a valid argument.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A diluted argument" describes a weakened or watered-down argument, which is a literal-sounding but incorrect interpretation of the idiom.

• Option 2: "Appear to be of no value" is the opposite of the idiom's actual meaning.

• Option 3: "Stop emphasising a point" is unrelated to the true sense of testing an argument's validity.

NOTE

• Other water-related idioms tested by SSC: "To test the water(s)" (to try something cautiously before committing), "In hot water" (in trouble), "To keep one's head above water" (to just about manage financially), "Water under the bridge" (past events that are no longer important).

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence.
Rajib's research aims to identify the strings that connect man and nature in order to provide a comprehensive examination and asessment of a variety of ecological issues.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. asessment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "assessment" — meaning the evaluation or estimation of the nature, quality or ability of someone/something.
◦ Example: The teacher's assessment of the student's progress was very positive.

• Spelling key: AS + SESS + MENT — note the double "s" after "as-" (assess → assessment). The given word wrongly drops one "s".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "strings" is spelt correctly.

• Option 2: "ecological" is spelt correctly.

• Option 4: "comprehensive" is spelt correctly.

NOTE

• Words built on "assess" that need the double "s": assessment, assessor, assessable.

• Other commonly misspelt double-letter words: necessary, possession, embarrassment, professional, occurrence.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The concert sounded was in cacophony with every instrument playing in synchronisation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. harmony.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Cacophony" means a harsh, jarring mixture of discordant sounds. (कर्कश ध्वनि, स्वरों का कोलाहल)
◦ Example: The cacophony of car horns in the traffic jam gave her a headache.

• Its antonym "Harmony" means a pleasing, consistent combination or agreement of sounds, especially musical notes played together. (सामंजस्य, सुर-ताल की एकरूपता)
◦ Example: The choir sang in perfect harmony.

• The sentence describes "every instrument playing in synchronisation", which logically corresponds to harmony, not to a clashing, discordant sound — confirming this contextual fit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Alimony (गुजारा भत्ता): Money paid by one spouse to another after separation/divorce; unrelated in meaning to sound.

• Option 3: Bedlam (अफरा-तफरी, हंगामा): A scene of uproar and confusion; this is actually closer to a synonym, not antonym, of cacophony.

• Option 4: Euphony (श्रुतिमधुरता): A pleasant, agreeable sound — while this is also an antonym of cacophony in a general sense, "harmony" is the better contextual fit here because the sentence specifically refers to instruments playing together in sync, which describes harmony rather than pleasant sound in general.

NOTE

• Word family: cacophony (harsh sound) vs euphony/harmony (pleasant sound); cacology (bad choice of words) vs eulogy (words of praise) — SSC often tests such Greek-root opposite pairs beginning with "caco-" (bad) and "eu-" (good).

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Back in April
P. an afternoon walking around
Q. the Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve
R. I was visiting family in South Carolina
S. and my brother and I spent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. RSPQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Read all four parts along with the fixed opening "Back in April" to identify the logical chronological/narrative flow.

• R. "I was visiting family in South Carolina" logically follows "Back in April" — it sets the scene (when and where the speaker was).

• S. "and my brother and I spent" follows naturally from R, continuing the same sentence with "and", introducing who performed the next action.

• P. "an afternoon walking around" follows S, completing the verb "spent" with what the afternoon was spent doing.

• Q. "the Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve" follows P, completing "walking around" with the specific place.

• Full sentence: "Back in April, I was visiting family in South Carolina, and my brother and I spent an afternoon walking around the Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: QPRS is incorrect because it begins with "the Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve" right after "Back in April", which does not make grammatical or logical sense.

• Option 3: PQRS is incorrect because "an afternoon walking around" cannot logically follow "Back in April" without first establishing who was where.

• Option 4: RQPS is incorrect because it places "the Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve" (Q) immediately after South Carolina (R), breaking the required "spent an afternoon walking around" construction.

NOTE

• In para/sentence-jumbling questions, look first for a part that logically follows the fixed opening (introduction of subject/setting), and for connecting words like "and", pronouns, and articles that link two parts together.

question:
Select the appropriate adverb for the underlined word in the sentence.
I complete forgot her birthday, and I don’t know how to make it up to her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. completely.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word "complete" modifies the verb "forgot" in the sentence, but "complete" is an adjective, and adjectives cannot modify verbs — only adverbs can.

• Rule: To modify a verb, an adverb (usually formed by adding -ly to the adjective) must be used.
◦ Adjective: complete → Adverb: completely

• Corrected sentence: "I completely forgot her birthday, and I don't know how to make it up to her."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "completeness" is a noun (the state of being complete); a noun cannot modify a verb.

• Option 2: "completed" is the past tense/past participle of the verb "complete"; using it here would create two verbs without a conjunction, which is ungrammatical.

• Option 3: "completing" is the present participle/gerund form of the verb; it cannot function as an adverb modifying "forgot".

NOTE

• Common adjective-to-adverb pairs tested by SSC: quick → quickly, careful → carefully, happy → happily, sudden → suddenly. Always check whether the word being modified is a noun (needs an adjective) or a verb/adjective/other adverb (needs an adverb).

question:
Select the correct direct form of the given sentence.
My teacher forbids to trust one’s relatives.
option_1: My teacher says, “Never trust your relatives.”
option_2: My teacher says, “Never trust my relatives.”
option_3: My teacher says, “Never trusted your relatives.”
option_4: My teacher said “Never trust your relatives.”
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. My teacher says, “Never trust your relatives.”

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The indirect sentence "My teacher forbids to trust one's relatives" is a negative imperative (order/advice) in indirect speech, introduced by the reporting verb "forbids".

• Rule — Indirect to Direct, Imperative sentences with "forbid": When the reporting verb is "forbid/forbids/forbade", the direct speech is converted into a negative command using "Never" / "Do not", and the reporting verb becomes "says/said" (or "told... not to").
◦ Indirect: Subject + forbids/forbade + to + V1
◦ Direct: Subject + says/said, "Never + V1..."

• Since the reporting verb is in the Simple Present ("forbids"), the reporting verb in direct speech must also remain in the Simple Present ("says"), and the possessive "one's" (referring generally to the listener) becomes "your" in the direct command addressed to the relatives' owner.
◦ Direct: My teacher says, "Never trust your relatives."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Never trust my relatives" is incorrect because "one's" refers to the person being advised (i.e., the listener), which becomes "your", not "my".

• Option 3: "Never trusted your relatives" is incorrect because a command/imperative always uses the base form of the verb ("trust"), never the past tense ("trusted").

• Option 4: "My teacher said..." is incorrect because the reporting verb in the given indirect sentence is "forbids" (Simple Present), so the direct speech reporting verb must also be "says", not "said" (Simple Past).

NOTE

• Other reporting verbs that introduce negative commands in direct speech similarly: "prohibit", "warn... not to", "order... not to".

• Remember: tense of the reporting verb ("says" vs "said") must match between indirect and direct speech — it does not change during this conversion.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Repulsive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Pleasant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Repulsive" means causing intense distaste or disgust; extremely unpleasant. (घृणित, प्रतिकर्षक)
◦ Example: The smell from the drain was repulsive.

• Its antonym "Pleasant" means giving a sense of enjoyment or satisfaction; agreeable. (सुखद, मनभावन)
◦ Example: They spent a pleasant evening by the lake.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Steadfast (दृढ़, अटल): Firmly fixed or unwavering in loyalty/purpose; relates to constancy, not attractiveness.

• Option 2: Superfluous (अनावश्यक, अतिरिक्त): More than what is needed; unnecessary — unrelated to how pleasant or disgusting something is.

• Option 4: Hopeless (निराशाजनक): Having or offering no hope; describes despair, not attractiveness/disgust.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "repulsive": revolting, repugnant, disgusting, loathsome.

• Other antonyms of "repulsive": attractive, appealing, charming, delightful.

question:
Select the correct passive voice form for the given sentence.
Sudha was writing a letter to her husband.
option_1: A letter were been written by Sudha to her husband.
option_2: A letter were being written by Sudha to her husband.
option_3: A letter was been written by Sudha to her husband.
option_4: A letter was being written by Sudha to her husband.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A letter was being written by Sudha to her husband.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Sudha was writing a letter to her husband" is in the Past Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + was/were + V-ing + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + being + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "a letter" becomes the subject (singular, so "was"); "being" is inserted; "writing" becomes the past participle "written"; and "Sudha" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: A letter was being written by Sudha to her husband.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "were been written" is grammatically impossible — "were" and "been" cannot occur together in this way, and "letter" (singular) cannot take "were".

• Option 2: "were being written" wrongly uses the plural auxiliary "were" with the singular subject "a letter" (should be "was").

• Option 3: "was been written" incorrectly combines "was" and "been", which is not a valid passive construction; the continuous marker "being" is missing.

NOTE

• Subject-verb agreement is critical in passive voice: a singular object (like "a letter") always takes was, never "were", when converted into the passive subject.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Something that is very small/little
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Tiny.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Tiny" means very small in size or amount. (बहुत छोटा, नन्हा)
◦ Example: A tiny kitten was hiding under the sofa.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Few (कुछ, थोड़े): A small number of countable things; refers to quantity/number, not physical size.

• Option 3: Thin (पतला): Having a small distance between opposite sides/surfaces, or (of a person) not fat; describes shape/build, not overall smallness.

• Option 4: Slender (छरहरा, दुबला-पतला): Gracefully thin, especially of a person's build; also about shape, not overall smallness.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "tiny": minute, miniature, minuscule, diminutive, petite.

• Do not confuse "few" (small number, used with countable nouns) with "little" (small amount, used with uncountable nouns) — a frequent SSC grammar trap.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A great fire (1)______ in London in 1666 which (2)____ the city and made around 1,00,000 people homeless. This fire is said to have begun in a pudding lane. It (3)____ through the crowded streets and wooden houses. However, after the fire, London was (4)___ with wider streets and improved water supplies. New buildings were (5)___ using bricks instead of wood.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. broke out.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Break out" is a phrasal verb meaning (of something unwelcome, such as a fire, war or disease) to start or begin suddenly.
◦ Example: A fire broke out in the factory late at night.

• Since the passage describes a great fire starting in London in 1666, the phrasal verb "broke out" (past tense of "break out") correctly fits blank 1.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "broke for" is not a standard phrasal verb combination and does not fit the context of a fire starting.

• Option 2: "broke in" means to enter a building by force (as in a burglary), or to interrupt someone speaking; it does not mean "to start suddenly".

• Option 4: "broke at" is not a recognised phrasal verb combination in English.

NOTE

• Other common "break" phrasal verbs: break down (to stop functioning, or to become emotionally overwhelmed), break up (to end a relationship, or to separate into pieces), break away (to escape or separate from a group).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A great fire (1)______ in London in 1666 which (2)____ the city and made around 1,00,000 people homeless. This fire is said to have begun in a pudding lane. It (3)____ through the crowded streets and wooden houses. However, after the fire, London was (4)___ with wider streets and improved water supplies. New buildings were (5)___ using bricks instead of wood.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. destroyed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Destroy" means to severely damage something so that it no longer exists or works, ending it completely.
◦ Example: The earthquake destroyed hundreds of homes.

• The passage states the fire "made around 1,00,000 people homeless" — this large-scale devastation is best described by "destroyed the city", the most natural and widely-used collocation for a city ravaged by fire.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "smashed" typically refers to breaking a solid object violently into pieces (e.g., smashed a window); it does not naturally collocate with "city" in this sense.

• Option 3: "shattered" typically describes glass, hopes, or dreams breaking suddenly into pieces; it is not the idiomatic word used for a city devastated by fire.

• Option 4: "demolished" usually refers to the deliberate, planned pulling down of a building/structure (e.g., by machinery); it does not fit the sense of accidental, sweeping destruction caused by a fire as naturally as "destroyed".

NOTE

• "Destroy" is the general, most versatile verb for large-scale ruin caused by disasters (fires, floods, wars, earthquakes) and is the standard word used in historical accounts of the Great Fire of London.

New buildings were (5)___ using bricks instead of wood.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. swept.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Sweep through" is a phrasal expression meaning to spread rapidly and forcefully through a place, commonly used for fires, storms, epidemics, etc.
◦ Example: The wildfire swept through the dry forest within hours.

• Since the passage describes the fire spreading rapidly "through the crowded streets and wooden houses", "swept" is the standard collocation for a fire's rapid, forceful spread.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "glided" means to move smoothly and effortlessly, usually without friction (e.g., a skater glides); it does not convey the destructive, rapid spread of a fire.

• Option 2: "carried" means to transport or support the weight of something; "it carried through the streets" is not idiomatic in this context.

• Option 4: "pulled" means to apply force to move something towards oneself; it does not describe a fire spreading through an area.

NOTE

• Other words commonly collocated with fires/disasters spreading: "rage" (the fire raged for days), "ravage" (the storm ravaged the coastline), "engulf" (flames engulfed the building).

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

A great fire (1)______ in London in 1666 which (2)____ the city and made around 1,00,000 people homeless. This fire is said to have begun in a pudding lane. It (3)____ through the crowded streets and wooden houses. However, after the fire, London was (4)___ with wider streets and improved water supplies. New buildings were (5)___ using bricks instead of wood.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. rebuilt.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Rebuild" means to build something again after it has been damaged or destroyed.
◦ Example: The village was rebuilt after the flood, with stronger flood defences.

• Since the passage explains that "after the fire, London was ___ with wider streets and improved water supplies", the city being constructed anew (after destruction) is correctly expressed by "rebuilt".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "innovated" means to introduce new methods, ideas or products; it does not mean physically reconstructing a city after destruction.

• Option 3: "modelled" means to design or shape something according to a pattern; "London was modelled with wider streets" does not fit the sense of reconstruction after a disaster.

• Option 4: "restored" means to bring something back to its former/original condition; however, the passage specifies London was given wider streets and improved water supplies — i.e. changed/improved, not simply returned to its original state — so "rebuilt" (built anew, differently) fits better than "restored".

NOTE

• Distinguish "rebuild" (construct again, often differently/better) from "restore" (return to the original/former condition) and "renovate" (repair and improve an existing structure without necessarily changing its design).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Erect" means to construct or build something, typically referring to buildings, walls or structures, by putting it up vertically.
◦ Example: New office towers were erected in the city centre.

• Since the passage says "New buildings were ___ using bricks instead of wood", the standard verb used for constructing buildings from a specified material is "erected".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "organised" means to arrange or coordinate systematically; it does not mean physically constructing a building.

• Option 3: "fabricated" means to manufacture or construct, but more commonly refers to industrial/mechanical assembly (e.g., fabricated parts) or, in another sense, to invent a false story; it is not the natural collocation for constructing buildings from bricks.

• Option 4: "located" means to be situated in or discover the position of something; it does not mean "to build" and does not fit the sense of buildings being constructed with bricks.

NOTE

• Common verbs for constructing structures: erect, construct, build, put up — all can be used with buildings; "erect" is especially common in formal/historical writing about walls, monuments and buildings.
